articles.author: Gaurav Asawa
articles.description:
I Built a State Management Library That Works Like React's useState — Meet CreateStore


If you've worked with React, you've probably used useState countless times.
It's simple, predictable, and gets the job done.
But as an application grows, things get a little more complicated. You have components deeply nested in the component tree that need access to the same state. Suddenly, you're passing props through multiple components, introducing Context Providers, or bringing in a state management library with its own concepts and boilerplate.
I kept thinking:
Why can't sharing global state be as simple as using useState?
That question led me to build CreateStore, a JavaScript state management library that I've recently published on npm.
In this article, I'll walk through the problem, how Creat…
articles.title: I Built a State Management Library That Works Like React's useState

articles.description:
Nod can provide a single assistant experience across laptops, desktops, and hosted machines, but only when each client connects to the same Nod server. In that setup, the server is the home for the assistant and its shared state. Separate local installations, or clients attached to different servers, do not automatically combine their memory.
The distinction matters for anyone expecting an AI assistant to retain context while they move between devices. Nod's official desktop installation documentation instructs users who already have a Nod server to select Connect to a server during setup. Once connected, clients reach the same assistant and connected accounts rather than creating separate assistant environments on every computer.
Nod's server connection is not a file-sync feature between …

articles.author: TECHDEV
articles.description:
My AI shipped a 1,199-line change nobody understood. I built a CLI that scores how fragile it is.


An essay made the rounds this week: "AI usage generates a fragile codebase." The argument is simple. AI writes code faster than humans can review it, so the bottleneck moved from writing to the review gate. Code that looks right, passes the easy tests, and ships before anyone understands it.
I have felt that exact failure mode. A 1,199-line change lands, the tests are green, the diff is too big to read properly, and two weeks later nobody on the team can explain what half of it does. The review happened. Understanding did not.
So I built fragility: a zero-dependency TypeScript CLI that measures four fragility modes of AI-written code on the diff you are about to merge, and returns a CI verdi…
articles.title: My AI shipped a 1,199-line change nobody understood. I built a CLI that scores how fragile it is.

articles.author: FDE at Trida AI
articles.description:
Originally published at Trida AI.
The dangerous moment in an agent run is not the first failed tool call. It is the fortieth.
A person whose lookup tool times out twice tries something else, or goes and makes tea. An agent does neither. It replans, and the new plan starts with the same lookup. It rewords the arguments and calls again, because from where it sits, each attempt looks like a fresh idea. The retries built into the tool layer add their own attempts underneath. None of these callers is misbehaving. Every one of them is doing exactly what it was told to do, which is to get the information and finish the task. Together they aim a steady stream of calls at a service that has already said, several times, that it cannot answer.
That stream is not harmless. Google's SRE book defines a …
articles.title: Circuit Breakers for Agent Tools

articles.author: Maxime Saint-joannis
articles.description:
Every day, agents pick tools for us. A skill to write a document, an MCP server to read a database, a paid endpoint for some data. Many of these calls work. Some fail quietly: the skill needed a key nobody had set, the server answered with nothing useful, the endpoint took the payment and returned an empty body. The agent moves on, and the next agent facing the same choice starts from zero.
What strikes me is not that tools fail. It is that the knowledge of how they fail, and for whom, disappears at the end of each session. The agent that found out does not keep it, and nobody else ever sees it.
Each actor around an agent sees a slice. A registry knows a tool exists and how it describes itself. A scanner knows what its code contains. A check before payment sees an endpoint at the moment it…
articles.title: Why does no agent remember what worked?

articles.description:
Bitcoin is presented as the first cryptocurrency. It is a decentralized digital currency with a fixed supply of 21 million coins, a peer-to-peer network, Proof of Work security, and transparent but pseudonymous transactions.
The important beginner idea is not only that Bitcoin is digital money. It is that Bitcoin showed how a network could record value transfers without relying on a single company, government, or bank to update the ledger.
